claims.text: The equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Identical thermomechanical processing and annealing protocols will produce comparable grain sizes and initial microstructures across the alloys.
Mechanical-property differences among the alloys are primarily caused by composition-induced variations in stacking fault energy.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has lower stacking fault energy than its quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
Lower stacking fault energy in the quinary alloy promotes deformation twinning.
Lower stacking fault energy in the quinary alloy promotes extended partial-dislocation slip.
Twinning and extended partial slip enhance strain hardening and delay failure in the quinary alloy.
The higher-SFE quaternary and ternary alloys favor dominant planar slip.
Dominant planar slip in the quaternary and ternary alloys causes earlier strain localization.
Changes in elemental makeup caused by reducing constituent count alter intrinsic stacking fault energy.
Stacking fault energy modulates deformation-twin formation and the width of dislocation dissociation zones.
Weak-beam TEM and twin-thickness analysis can be used to estimate stacking fault energy and document deformation-twin density.
The comparison should use room-temperature deformation at controlled strain rates and identical processing histories.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at extreme temperatures or strain rates.
Under identical tensile-test conditions, the quinary alloy will exhibit a higher deformation-twin density than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Under identical tensile-test conditions, the quinary alloy will exhibit wider stacking-fault regions than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in both twin density and stacking-fault width in the quinary alloy would falsify the proposed SFE mechanism.
